lessons.title: Can, can't and basic requests
objectives: Express simple present ability using can and can't.
Ask about ability and give short answers.
Make a polite basic request with Can you ... please?
Use the base form of a verb after can or can't.

explanation.en: Can expresses an ability now: I can ride a bike. Can't or cannot expresses lack of ability: She can't swim yet. Can does not change after he, she or it, and the next verb stays in its base form: He can draw, not 'cans draws'. Questions put can before the subject: Can you swim? Yes, I can. No, I can't. A polite everyday request can use Can you open the window, please? Read whether the sentence asks about ability or requests help. For gap tasks, type only the missing word or phrase.
explanation.vi: Can diễn tả khả năng hiện tại, can't/cannot là chưa thể làm được. Sau can/can't dùng động từ nguyên mẫu, không thêm -s hoặc to. Đảo can lên trước chủ ngữ để hỏi. Lời nhờ lịch sự: Can you ... please? Chỉ điền phần thiếu.

examples: ABILITY · Nia can ride a bicycle now.
NO ABILITY · Ben can't swim yet; he is learning.
QUESTION · Can you draw a map? Yes, I can.
REQUEST · Can you pass me the notebook, please?
FORM · She can sing, not 'she cans sings'.
GAP · My brother ___ (not / swim) yet. → can't swim / cannot swim.

items.prompt: Lina has learned to swim and can swim across the pool. Choose the sentence that reports her ability.

feedback.explanation_en: Can is followed by the base verb swim. Do not add -s after can, use swimming after can, or omit to from is able to swim.

items.author_action: Use plausible verb-form errors rather than impossible word order.

items.prompt: Use can/can't to describe present ability. Complete with the missing phrase only: My little brother has not learned to ride yet; he ___ (not / ride) a bicycle.

feedback.explanation_en: The task specifically asks for ability with can/can't. Use can't ride or cannot ride, followed by the base verb ride. 'Doesn't ride' is grammatical elsewhere, but it does not use the requested modal form.

items.author_action: State can/can't ability target; don't reject natural habitual don't ride outside the target.

items.prompt: Which request to a classmate is the most polite?

options.text: Can you pass me the pencil, please?
Can you pass me the pencil?
You must pass me the pencil.

feedback.explanation_en: All the sentences ask for or demand the pencil, but Can you ... please? combines a question with please and is the most polite in this context. An imperative is more direct.

items.author_action: Ask for the MOST polite request; compare direct commands and questions.

items.prompt: Complete with can (write the missing word only): ___ you help me carry these books, please?

feedback.explanation_en: The instruction specifies can. Put Can before you to make a basic polite request. Could/would/will can be natural requests elsewhere, but this gap practises can specifically.

items.author_action: Explicitly constrain the word to can; other polite auxiliaries are possible elsewhere.

items.prompt: Choose the correct short answer: Can your sister play chess? (She has not learned yet.)

feedback.explanation_en: Can questions take can/can't in the short answer; the context says she has not learned.

items.prompt: Complete: She ___ (can / draw) animals very well.

feedback.explanation_en: Can is unchanged with she and is followed by the base verb draw.

items.prompt: Choose the correct form after can.

feedback.explanation_en: Use can play, without third-person -s, -ing or cans.

items.prompt: Complete: ___ he play chess? Yes, he can.

feedback.explanation_en: The ability question begins with Can. Do not repeat he, which is already printed.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly says that two children have the ability to read?

feedback.explanation_en: Can stays the same with plural subjects; read is the base verb.

items.prompt: Use can/can't to describe present ability. Complete with the missing phrase only: I have never learned German; I ___ (not / speak) it yet.

feedback.explanation_en: This task specifically practises can/can't for ability: can't speak or cannot speak. In other contexts don't speak is grammatical, but it does not use the requested modal form.

items.author_action: Explicitly constrain ability via can/can't rather than reject grammatical don't speak.

lessons.title: Past simple forms, negatives and questions
objectives: Use regular and common irregular verbs for finished past events.
Form negatives with didn't + base verb.
Make questions with Did + subject + base verb.
Use was/were for past forms of be and distinguish them from did.

explanation.en: The past simple describes a completed event at a stated or understood past time: We visited the museum yesterday. Most regular verbs take -ed, while common irregular verbs change form: go → went, buy → bought. For an ordinary action-verb negative, use didn't/did not + the base verb: We didn't go, not 'didn't went'. Questions use Did + subject + base verb: Did you visit? Past be is different: I/he/she was; you/we/they were. Do not add did to 'was/were' questions. A past-time phrase helps, but check which action the sentence describes. Type only the missing phrase in a gap.
explanation.vi: Quá khứ đơn diễn tả việc đã kết thúc. Động từ thường thêm -ed hoặc có dạng bất quy tắc (go → went). Phủ định dùng didn't + V nguyên mẫu, câu hỏi Did + chủ ngữ + V nguyên mẫu. Be ở quá khứ dùng was/were, không thêm did trước was/were.

examples: FINISHED · We visited the museum yesterday.
IRREGULAR · She went home after the match.
NEGATIVE · I didn't watch the film last night.
QUESTION · Did you go to the art club?
BE · He was late; they were early.
GAP · They ___ (not / play) yesterday. → didn't play / did not play.

items.prompt: Complete: We ___ the museum yesterday afternoon.

feedback.explanation_en: Yesterday afternoon gives a completed past time; visited is the regular past form of visit.

items.prompt: Complete in the past simple; enter the missing phrase only: I ___ (not / watch) television last night.

feedback.explanation_en: Use didn't/did not + base verb watch for the past simple negative. Past continuous could fit a different situation, but the requested tense here is past simple.

items.author_action: State past-simple target; don't treat past continuous as universally wrong.

items.prompt: Which question asks about a finished event last Sunday?

options.text: Did you go to the market last Sunday?
Do you went to the market last Sunday?
Did you went to the market last Sunday?
Are you go to the market last Sunday?

feedback.explanation_en: Did + subject + base verb go forms a past-simple action question.

items.prompt: Complete: Yesterday, Maya ___ (buy) a new notebook.

feedback.explanation_en: Buy is irregular: the past simple is bought, not buyed.

items.prompt: Choose the correct negative sentence.

feedback.explanation_en: The past-simple negative of an action verb is didn't + base verb play.

items.prompt: Complete: Where ___ you go last weekend?

feedback.explanation_en: The printed subject and base verb are already present: Where did you go ...?

items.prompt: Complete: Last month, our class ___ on a school trip.

feedback.explanation_en: Go has the irregular past form went, used for a finished past trip.

items.prompt: Complete: They ___ (be) at the library yesterday.

feedback.explanation_en: They takes were in the past simple of be. Do not add did.

items.prompt: Choose the correct past-simple question using be.

feedback.explanation_en: Past be questions invert was and the subject: Was she ...? Do not use did.

items.prompt: Use the past simple to complete the gap; enter the missing phrase only: She ___ (not / go) to the club last Tuesday.

feedback.explanation_en: The requested past-simple negative is didn't go or did not go. After did not, use the base verb go. Another tense needs different intended meaning.

items.author_action: State past-simple target; don't rule out contextual past continuous.

lessons.title: Countability, some/any, much/many
objectives: Distinguish common countable and uncountable nouns in everyday contexts.
Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns.
Use some in ordinary affirmative statements and any in neutral questions/negatives.
Choose a quantity expression based on both noun type and sentence meaning.

explanation.en: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms: one apple, three apples; ask how many apples. Uncountable nouns such as rice, water and milk do not normally take -s in these meanings; ask how much rice. Use some in ordinary affirmative statements: We have some bread. Any is common in neutral information questions and negatives: Are there any chairs? There aren't any chairs. Some can also appear in offers and requests when you expect a positive response, so always read the context rather than memorising an absolute rule. Use much with uncountable nouns and many with plural countable nouns. A unit phrase can make an uncountable substance countable: two bottles of water.
explanation.vi: Danh từ đếm được có dạng số ít/số nhiều; danh từ không đếm được như rice, water, milk thường không thêm -s theo nghĩa này. How many + số nhiều đếm được; how much + không đếm được. Some thường ở câu khẳng định, any thường ở câu hỏi trung tính/phủ định; vẫn có ngoại lệ theo mục đích nói.

examples: COUNTABLE · three apples; How many apples?
UNCOUNTABLE · some rice; How much rice?
AFFIRMATIVE · There are some books on the shelf.
NEGATIVE · There aren't any eggs in the box.
QUESTION · Are there any chairs in the hall?
UNIT · two bottles of water, not 'two waters' for two bottles.

items.prompt: Which noun is usually uncountable when it means food in general?

feedback.explanation_en: Rice names a substance in this meaning; the other options are countable items.

items.prompt: Complete: How ___ chairs are there in the hall?

feedback.explanation_en: Chairs is a plural countable noun, so use how many.

items.prompt: Complete: How ___ water do we need for the trip?

feedback.explanation_en: Water is uncountable in this context, so the quantity question uses how much.

items.prompt: Choose from some or any; type one word. The fridge is empty: there are zero eggs. There aren't ___ eggs in the fridge.

feedback.explanation_en: Use any (not some) in this negative statement to express that there are zero eggs. Many/enough would express a different quantity judgement, but the given choice is some or any.

items.author_action: Bound answer domain to some/any and explicitly say zero eggs.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses some naturally in an ordinary affirmative statement?

options.text: I have some apples in my bag.
I have any apples in my bag.
I have much apples in my bag.
I have an apples in my bag.

feedback.explanation_en: Some apples is natural in a simple affirmative statement with plural countable apples.

items.prompt: Choose from some or any; type one word. We need ___ oranges for the picnic; please add them to the shopping list.

feedback.explanation_en: Some fits this ordinary affirmative statement. The task limits the choice to some or any; other quantity words may work in different sentences, but they are not being tested here.

items.author_action: Bound answer domain to some/any for an ordinary affirmative statement.

items.prompt: A recipe needs milk as a liquid ingredient, not a café serving. Which noun phrase naturally refers to an unspecified amount?

feedback.explanation_en: Some milk treats milk as an uncountable ingredient in the recipe. A milk and three milks can name servings in a café, but not the intended uncountable quantity here.

items.author_action: Contextualize milk as liquid ingredient; acknowledge café serving sense.

items.prompt: Complete: How ___ milk is left in the bottle?

feedback.explanation_en: Milk is an uncountable liquid in this sentence; use how much.

items.prompt: Which expression clearly counts containers rather than the water itself?

feedback.explanation_en: Bottles is countable, so two bottles of water names two containers of an uncountable substance.

items.prompt: Choose from some or any; type one word. I have ___ rice at home and will use it for dinner.

feedback.explanation_en: Some fits an ordinary affirmative statement about rice. It describes an unspecified quantity, not proof that the amount is enough; this task contrasts some with any.

items.author_action: Constrain to some/any, remove false inference that some means enough.

lessons.title: Comparatives and superlatives
objectives: Use comparative forms with than for two people or things.
Use the + superlative for one item in a defined group of three or more.
Form common -er/-est and more/most patterns.
Use irregular better/best and worse/worst accurately.

explanation.en: To compare two things, often use an adjective's comparative form plus than: taller than; more interesting than. Many short adjectives use -er, and consonant + y changes to -ier: heavy → heavier. Longer adjectives often use more or most. A superlative identifies an extreme within a defined group: the tallest of three. The is generally used before the superlative in these examples. Common irregular forms include good → better → best and bad → worse → worst. Do not say 'more taller' or 'the most fastest'. For gap answers, enter only what replaces the blank.
explanation.vi: So sánh hơn giữa hai đối tượng thường dùng -er/more ... than. So sánh nhất trong một nhóm thường dùng the -est/the most ... . Heavy → heavier/heaviest; good → better/best; bad → worse/worst. Tránh dùng đồng thời more + -er hoặc most + -est.

examples: TWO · This pencil is longer than that one.
LONG ADJECTIVE · This story is more interesting than the first.
THREE · Of the three bags, the blue bag is the lightest.
SPELLING · heavy → heavier → heaviest.
IRREGULAR · good → better → best.
CONTRAST · taller than, not 'more taller than'.

items.prompt: Complete: Mai is ___ than her brother.

feedback.explanation_en: Than compares two people, so the comparative form taller is needed.

items.prompt: Complete: This schoolbag is ___ (heavy) than that one.

feedback.explanation_en: Heavy ends in consonant + y; change y to i and add -er for heavier.

items.prompt: Which sentence selects one book as the most interesting of three?

options.text: This is the most interesting of the three books.
This is more interesting of the three books.
This is the more interesting of the three books.
This is the most interesting than the other two books.

feedback.explanation_en: A group of three calls for the superlative the most interesting of the three. The comparative more interesting needs than and a specific comparison; a superlative is not followed by than here.

items.prompt: Complete: Of the three buses, the red one is the ___ (fast).

feedback.explanation_en: The fastest is the superlative within a group of three buses; the is already printed.

items.prompt: Complete: This answer is ___ than my first answer.

feedback.explanation_en: Good has the irregular comparative better; do not combine more and better.

items.prompt: Complete: Of all four posters, I think this is the ___ (good).

feedback.explanation_en: Good changes to best for a superlative in the defined group of four posters.

items.prompt: Which phrase correctly compares how exciting two events are?

feedback.explanation_en: Use more exciting than to compare the quality of two events. Most exciting is a superlative, while excited generally describes a person's feeling, not the event's quality.

items.author_action: Contrast event quality exciting with person feeling excited.

items.prompt: Complete: This book is ___ (interesting) than the first one.

feedback.explanation_en: Interesting commonly takes more for comparison of two books, not -er.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a superlative naturally?

options.text: My bag is the lightest of the three.
My bag is lighter of the three.
My bag is the more lightest of the three.
My bag is most lighter of the three.

feedback.explanation_en: The lightest correctly selects the extreme in a group of three.

items.prompt: Complete: Today the weather is ___ (bad) than yesterday.

feedback.explanation_en: Bad has irregular comparative worse; than shows a comparison between two days.

lessons.title: Travel and event collocations in context
objectives: Recognise frequent travel and event word partnerships in context.
Distinguish book a ticket, catch/miss a bus and pack a bag.
Use take photos and attend an event naturally.
Select a collocation from the meaning of the whole situation.

explanation.en: A collocation is a word partnership often used together. We book a ticket to reserve a seat, pack a bag before leaving, catch a bus when we get on in time, and miss a bus if it leaves before we arrive. We arrive at a station but arrive in a city. At an event, we may attend a workshop and take photos. Read the time and purpose in each sentence, not just the nearest noun. Other phrases may be grammatical in different situations, so select the expression that fits the stated meaning.
explanation.vi: Collocation là các từ thường đi với nhau. Book a ticket = đặt vé; pack a bag = xếp đồ; catch/miss a bus = bắt/lỡ xe. Arrive at a station nhưng arrive in a city. Attend a workshop và take photos. Xét cả ngữ cảnh trước khi chọn.

examples: BOOK · We booked two train tickets on Tuesday.
PACK · I packed my bag before the school trip.
CATCH · We left early to catch the eight o'clock bus.
MISS · The bus left without us; we missed it.
ARRIVE · Arrive at the station; arrive in the city.
EVENT · Attend a workshop and take photos afterward.

items.prompt: You want to reserve a train seat in advance, not check, cancel or simply pay for a ticket at the counter. Which phrase means make a reservation?

feedback.explanation_en: Book a ticket means reserve it in advance. Buy refers to paying, check to inspecting and cancel to ending the reservation; booking may also involve payment, but the question asks specifically about reserving.

items.author_action: Use plausible buy/check/cancel ticket alternatives and reservation-specific stem.

items.prompt: Choose from pack or book; type one word. Before a trip, please ___ your bag tonight by putting your clothes and notebook inside.

feedback.explanation_en: Pack a bag means put the items needed for a trip inside it. The task limits the choice to pack or book; book is used for reserving tickets or accommodation, not filling a bag.

items.author_action: Constrain choice to pack or book before travel.

items.prompt: You planned to take the eight o'clock bus, but it had already left when you reached the stop. Which sentence best describes what happened to that bus?

options.text: You caught the eight o'clock bus.
You missed the eight o'clock bus.
You waited at the stop for the eight o'clock bus before it left.
You arrived early and got on the eight o'clock bus.

feedback.explanation_en: You missed the eight o'clock bus because it departed before you arrived. The other choices would require arriving in time to catch or wait for that bus.

items.author_action: Describe one specific missed departure and compare realistic timing alternatives.

items.prompt: Which phrase gives the natural arrival expression for a station?

feedback.explanation_en: Arrive at is the normal expression for a specific point such as a station.

items.prompt: At the science fair, you pointed a camera at an exhibit and pressed the shutter. Which action did you perform?

feedback.explanation_en: Take photos means use the camera to create pictures. Looking, sharing and printing involve photos already taken; pressing the shutter is the taking action.

items.author_action: Contrast taking photos with looking at, sharing and printing.

items.prompt: You go to a weekend workshop as a student participant, not an organiser. Which action describes your role?

feedback.explanation_en: Attend a workshop means be present as a participant. Organise means plan it, cancel means call it off, and miss means not attend it.

items.prompt: Complete: We will ___ the bus if we do not leave now; it is already at the stop.

feedback.explanation_en: The bus may leave without us, so the natural phrase is miss the bus.

items.prompt: The organiser calls off the trip because the road is closed. The trip will not take place, and no later date is planned. Which action fits?

feedback.explanation_en: Cancel the trip means it will not take place. Postpone moves it to a later time; here no replacement date is planned.

items.author_action: Distinguish cancelled (no later date) from postponed.

lessons.title: A message about an art-club visit
objectives: Identify the sender's purpose in a short personal message.
Find an explicit meeting time and location.
Distinguish items the reader must bring from items supplied by the club.
Follow a simple changed plan and reply deadline.

explanation.en: Read the personal message and ask: Who is writing, why, where and when? Locate exact phrases for times and meeting places rather than guessing from the main event's starting time. Underline what the student must bring and what the club provides. Notice 'but' for a changed transport plan, 'if' for a condition and 'by Thursday' for the latest reply time. All answers should be supported by the message.
explanation.vi: Đọc tin nhắn, xác định ai viết, mục đích, giờ hẹn và địa điểm. Giờ gặp có thể khác giờ hoạt động bắt đầu. Phân biệt đồ phải mang theo và đồ được cung cấp. But thể hiện thay đổi, if là điều kiện, by Thursday là hạn chót.

examples: PURPOSE · The message makes plans for an art-club activity.
TIME · The club starts at 10 a.m.; the friends meet earlier at 9:30.
PLACE · The meeting point is outside the school library.
BRING/PROVIDE · Bring a pencil and sketchbook; the club provides paints.
CONDITION · Eat in the park if dry, but in the hall if it rains.
DEADLINE · Reply by Thursday.

reading_asset.title: Lan's art-club message
reading_asset.body:
Hi Minh,
Our art club is meeting at the community hall on Saturday at 10 a.m. I planned to take the bus with you, but my father can give us a lift. Please meet me outside the school library at 9:30 a.m. Bring a pencil and your sketchbook. You don't need to bring paints because the club will provide them. We will design postcards for a local exhibition. After the activity, we can have lunch in the park if it is dry. If it rains, we will eat in the hall instead. I must leave by 2 p.m. to visit my grandmother. Could you reply by Thursday so I can tell the club leader how many people are coming?
See you,
Lan

items.prompt: Why does Lan write to Minh?

options.text: To arrange their visit to an art-club activity
To arrange lunch only, not the club visit
To ask Minh to buy paints for the club
To announce that the library meeting place has changed to the park

feedback.explanation_en: Lan's main purpose is to arrange an art-club visit and receive Minh's reply. Lunch and supplies are supporting details; the message says the club provides paints and the meeting place is still the library.

items.prompt: Where should Minh meet Lan?

feedback.explanation_en: The message explicitly gives outside the school library as their meeting point.

items.prompt: When should the two friends meet?

feedback.explanation_en: The meeting is at 9:30 a.m., before the club starts at 10 a.m.

items.prompt: What alternative to taking the bus does Lan mention?

options.text: Her father can give them a lift
A bus supplied by the art club

feedback.explanation_en: Lan says her father can give them a lift. Can describes an available alternative; the message does not confirm a final travel decision or state a vehicle type.

items.author_action: Question asks for possible alternative exactly as stated, not a confirmed plan/vehicle.

items.prompt: Which items should Minh bring?

feedback.explanation_en: The message asks Minh to bring a pencil and his sketchbook.

items.prompt: Does Minh need to bring paints?

options.text: Yes, he must buy new paints.
No, the club will provide them.
Yes, because the club has no paints.
No, because nobody will paint or draw.

feedback.explanation_en: The message states the club provides the paints, so bringing them is unnecessary.

items.author_action: Remove inference tag because paint provision is explicit detail.

items.prompt: What will happen if it rains after the activity?

options.text: They will eat in the hall.
They will eat in the park anyway.
The friends must return to school immediately.
The event starts two hours earlier.

feedback.explanation_en: The conditional plan says they will eat in the hall if it rains.

items.prompt: What is the latest day Lan asks Minh to reply?

feedback.explanation_en: The message says reply by Thursday so Lan can confirm numbers with the leader.

lessons.title: Describe a familiar person or place
objectives: Identify the reader and required points in a short description.
Select relevant facts about one familiar person or place.
Connect simple sentences in a clear order.
Check the description independently before adult review.

explanation.en: First read the prompt and choose ONE subject: a familiar person at school or a familiar place at school. For a person, plan who they are, what they do and why you appreciate them. For a place, plan where it is, what you can see there and why you like it. Brainstorm short facts; select details that answer the chosen task. Write a clear opening and three or four connected sentences; then check capital letters, be, there is/are, simple present forms and punctuation. Use a made-up name if needed and do not include private contact details. Your own paragraph, not your word count, is the evidence for adult review.
explanation.vi: Đọc đề và chọn MỘT đối tượng: người quen ở trường hoặc địa điểm trong trường. Với người: họ là ai, làm gì, vì sao em quý họ. Với nơi chốn: ở đâu, có gì, vì sao em thích. Brainstorm, chọn chi tiết liên quan, viết câu mở đầu và vài câu nối tiếp, rồi tự kiểm tra. Không đưa thông tin liên hệ riêng tư; bài viết cần người lớn đánh giá.

examples: TASK · Describe a person OR a place at school, not both.
PERSON PLAN · My librarian → helps pupils → friendly → why I like her.
PLACE PLAN · School library → next to hall → books and tables → why I like it.
PLACE MODEL · My favourite place is our school library. It is next to the hall. There are many books and two large tables. I like it because I can read quietly with my friends.
PERSON MODEL · Mr Nam works in our school library. He helps students find books. He is patient and kind. I like him because he explains things clearly.
SELF-CHECK · Is every sentence about my chosen subject? Are the verbs and punctuation clear?

items.prompt: The task asks you to describe ONE familiar person or place. Which plan follows the task?

options.text: Choose one subject, select relevant facts and note why you like it.
Describe both a person and a place even though the task asks for one.
Choose a person but use only unrelated details about a different event.
Choose a place but list names of other pupils instead of describing its features.

feedback.explanation_en: The task requires one chosen subject with relevant details and a personal reason. Mixing subjects or replacing its details with unrelated information does not fulfil the prompt.

items.prompt: You chose to describe the school library. Which detail is relevant?

options.text: My uncle bought a bicycle yesterday.
The bus arrives in another city.
I forgot my sports shoes at home.

feedback.explanation_en: The tables tell the reader something concrete about the chosen place.

items.prompt: Which outline gives the clearest order for a short description of one school place?

options.text: Opening → location → features → why I like it
Location → one feature → opening → why I like it
Opening → personal reason → unrelated holiday event → ending
Opening → place features → unrelated person → location

feedback.explanation_en: Start by introducing the same place, tell the reader where it is, develop its features and end with a reason. Other outlines delay the opening or interrupt the description with unrelated content.

items.author_action: Compare realistic outline orders with topic cohesion.

items.prompt: Choose the sentence with correct basic grammar for describing the school library.

options.text: There are many books in the library.
There is many books in the library.
There are a books in the library.
There are many book in the library.

feedback.explanation_en: Books is plural, so use there are and the plural noun books.

items.prompt: Write one paragraph about EITHER a familiar person at school OR a place at school (real or imaginary). If you choose a person, explain who they are, what they do and why you like or appreciate them. If you choose a place, explain where it is, describe two features and say why you like it. Aim for about 40–60 words. Brainstorm three facts, make a short plan, then self-check your own paragraph. Do not include a private address, phone number or other personal contact details.

feedback.pending_message: Your paragraph is saved for adult review. Check the chosen subject and task details before revising; word count alone never determines your score.
